intro: Frank Lévy plays Chopin’s Ballade No. 4 in F minor, Op. 52, marked Andante con moto. A soft F-minor theme returns several times with more voices added around it, and five soft chords come before the coda.

sections.label: Intro · Repeated Gs over C major
sections.mNote: The melody falls from G to a held E.

sections.label: A · F-minor theme
sections.mNote: The melody returns with new ornaments and added voices.

sections.label: B · B♭-major melody in chords
sections.mNote: The piano plays the melody in chords, piano e dolce.

sections.label: Intro · Opening melody in A major
sections.mNote: The introductory melody returns and leads into a cadenza.

sections.label: A′ · First theme, imitative, D minor
sections.mNote: The first theme returns in D minor, then F minor.

sections.label: B′ · second theme, D♭ major, wide arpeggios
sections.mNote: The second theme returns over wide left-hand arpeggios.

sections.label: Link · Five slow chords over bass C
sections.mNote: A bass C is held beneath the slow-moving chords.

sections.label: Coda · F minor, semiquavers in both hands
sections.mNote: After the silence, both hands play rapid semiquaver figures.

cues.title: Opening in C major
cues.text: Repeated Gs sound high in the piano over harmony in C major. The melody falls, then rests on E. Chopin holds back F minor, the key of the Ballade, for seven bars.
cues.evidence: Chopin, Ballade Op. 52, Joseffy edition, bars 1–7: repeated G octaves, C-major harmony and the held E. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=422
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: First theme, F minor
cues.text: The first theme is in F minor, and its melody repeatedly moves by semitone to neighbouring notes. A quiet accompaniment rocks beneath it. When the phrase returns, Chopin adds turns and faster notes within the same line.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 8–36: first theme and its ornamented restatement; C–D♭–B♮–C at the opening of the theme.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Dedication to Charlotte de Rothschild
cues.text: Chopin dedicated the Fourth Ballade to Baroness Charlotte de Rothschild. He wrote it in 1842, a year after the Third. It was the last of his four works with the title.
cues.evidence: Date, dedicatee and place as the last Ballade: Mieczysław Tomaszewski, Fryderyk Chopin Institute. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor

cues.title: Second theme in B♭ major
cues.text: The second theme is in B♭ major, marked piano e dolce (softly and sweetly). The right hand plays a chordal melody above a rocking bass. Its phrases move in broader steps than the curling line of the first theme.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 80–99; Tomaszewski identifies the B♭-major sicilienne and piano e dolce marking. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Cortot and The Three Budrys
cues.text: In the preface to his edition of the Ballades, the pianist Alfred Cortot linked this one to Mickiewicz’s poem The Three Budrys, in which a father sends his three sons off to seek treasure and they come home with three Polish brides. Nothing Chopin wrote confirms it.
cues.evidence: Alfred Cortot’s attribution of the Fourth Ballade to Mickiewicz’s Trzech Budrysów, as reported in the preface to Chopin’s Letters, coll. Henryk Opienski, trans. E. L. Voynich (New York: Knopf, 1931), pp. vii–viii, whose translator adds that she knows of no authentic evidence for any of the Ballade–Mickiewicz links: https://archive.org/details/chopinsletters00chop. Cortot’s own foreword to the Salabert edition was not opened.

cues.title: Return of the introduction in A major
cues.text: In bars 129–134 the introductory melody returns in A major, with its repeated notes and falling phrase. The bass has moved from C to A. The piano then plays a cadenza, marked dolcissimo and rallentando, over a chord of A major.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 129–134: A-major return of the introduction and cadenza marked dolcissimo and rallentando.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the first theme, D minor
cues.text: The first theme returns in D minor, and the left hand imitates the right half a bar later. More voices enter as the music moves back to F minor.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 135–145: imitative return beginning A–B♭–D–C♯ in D minor, with the lower voice entering half a bar later; F-minor theme from bar 139.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Decorated return of the first theme
cues.text: At bars 152–168 the first theme returns with nocturne-like embellishments high on the keyboard, above the harmony. Jim Samson called it a “cantabile-decorative treatment of exquisitely moulded ornamental melody”.
cues.evidence: Jim Samson, Chopin: The Four Ballades (Cambridge University Press, 1992): “a cantabile-decorative treatment of exquisitely moulded ornamental melody” (found by full-text search at the Internet Archive; the page itself was not read). Joseffy edition (Mutopia Project), bars 152–168: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/ChopinFF/O52/ballade-4/ballade-4-lys/ballade-4.ly
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the second theme, D♭ major
cues.text: The second theme returns in D♭ major, first heard in B♭ major. The left hand plays wide arpeggios and the right hand carries the melody above in chords.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 169–191: second-theme return in D♭ major over wide left-hand arpeggios.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Five chords over C
cues.text: After the rush, five quiet chords sound over a bass C in bars 203–210. The upper notes change and the bass stays on C. The last chord, in C major, is tied across bars 207–210, and a silence follows before the coda.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 203–210: five chord attacks over C, with the final C-major chord tied across bars 207–210.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Coda, bar 211
cues.text: The coda follows a soft chord in C major and opens on a low F in the bass at bar 211. Semiquaver triplets alternate between the hands, with sharp accents and chromatic figuration, in the Ballade’s most strenuous writing in F minor.
cues.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 211 onwards: F bass at the coda’s opening, semiquaver triplets and accented chromatic figuration.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: From C-major introduction to F-minor theme
transitions.from: Intro · Repeated Gs over C major
transitions.how: The introduction holds E over C-major harmony and a fermata. A C pickup starts the first theme, which moves through F minor at a tempo. Beneath the quieter melody, the left hand takes up a regular accompaniment.

transitions.title: The second theme in B♭ major
transitions.how: The running notes of the first theme give way to a theme in B♭ major, marked piano e dolce. The right hand plays the melody in chords, with D as the top note, and the left hand moves back and forth between bass notes and accompanying chords.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 79–85; B♭-major sicilienne and marking also described by Tomaszewski at https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/115_ballade-in-f-minor.

transitions.title: Return of the introduction in A major
transitions.to: Intro · Opening melody in A major
transitions.how: The developing passage reaches A major, with A in the bass. Above it the introduction’s repeated-note melody returns. Its last phrase slows into a cadenza marked dolcissimo, and the cadenza’s arpeggios spread the A-major chord across both hands.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 128–134: A-major introductory return, dolcissimo cadenza and rallentando.

transitions.title: From the cadenza to the D-minor imitation
transitions.from: Intro · Opening melody in A major
transitions.to: A′ · First theme, imitative, D minor
transitions.how: In bars 134–140 the A-major cadenza ends under a fermata. The right hand begins the first theme in D minor, marked legato. Half a bar later the left hand repeats its opening notes in imitation. The harmony then moves back towards F minor.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 134–140: A-major cadenza, D-minor imitation and subsequent F-minor phrase.

transitions.title: Second song returns in D♭ major
transitions.from: A′ · First theme, imitative, D minor
transitions.to: B′ · second theme, D♭ major, wide arpeggios
transitions.how: The decorated phrases of the first theme lead into the second song in D♭ major (bars 168–175 in the Joseffy edition). The left hand plays wide arpeggios, and the right hand plays the melody above them in chords. The melody keeps its original rhythm over the larger accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 168–175: D♭-major second-theme return and wide left-hand arpeggios.

transitions.title: The bass stops on C
transitions.from: B′ · second theme, D♭ major, wide arpeggios
transitions.to: Link · Five slow chords over bass C
transitions.how: In bars 201–210 of the Joseffy edition, the fast passage ends on a C-major chord, followed by a rest with a fermata. Five quiet chords follow. A low C stays in the bass while their upper notes change, and the last chord, again C major, is held across several bars.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 201–210: C-major cadence, rest with fermata, and five quiet chords above a C bass.

transitions.title: Held C-major chord to the coda
transitions.from: Link · Five slow chords over bass C
transitions.to: Coda · F minor, semiquavers in both hands
transitions.how: The held C-major chord is followed by rests. A low F begins the coda, and both hands leap into semiquaver triplets. The dominant harmony resolves to F minor. In the Joseffy edition the join spans bars 207–213.
transitions.evidence: Joseffy edition, bars 207–213: held C-major chord, rests, F bass and the coda’s semiquaver triplets.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
